rows.source: HSE work-related stress management standards
rows.verified: Employers have a legal duty to protect workers from work-related stress by assessing the risk and acting on it.

rows.source: HSE work-related stress management standards
rows.verified: HSE Management Standards use a step-by-step risk-assessment approach focused on preventing underlying causes of stress.

rows.source: HSE work-related stress management standards
rows.verified: The Management Standards cover demands, control, support, relationships, role and organisational change.

rows.source: HSE work-related stress management standards
rows.verified: Employers should use existing data, surveys and worker consultation to assess the current stress-risk situation.

rows.source: HSE work-related stress management standards
rows.verified: Worker and representative participation is needed to identify practical improvements and monitor their effectiveness.

rows.source: HSE work-related stress management standards
rows.verified: Stress controls should address work design and management rather than relying only on individual coping measures.

rows.source: HSE work-related stress management standards
rows.verified: Risk-assessment findings should be recorded, implemented, monitored and reviewed.

rows.source: HSE work-related stress management standards
rows.verified: HSE provides free workbooks, templates and guidance to support the Management Standards process.

rows.source: HSE work-related stress management standards
rows.verified: Work-related stress risk depends on job demands, control, support, relationships, role clarity, change, worker factors and organisational context.

rows.source: HSE work-related stress management standards
rows.verified: HSE stress evidence is organisation-, role-, worker-, control-, assessment- and time-specific and is not an exact parcel-level mental-health probability.

rows.source: HSE workplace heat-stress and thermal-comfort control
rows.verified: Heat stress occurs when the body's ability to control its internal temperature starts to fail.

rows.source: HSE workplace heat-stress and thermal-comfort control
rows.verified: Risk assessment should consider work rate, air temperature, humidity, air movement, radiant heat, clothing and personal protective equipment.

rows.source: HSE workplace heat-stress and thermal-comfort control
rows.verified: Heat-stress symptoms can include reduced concentration, cramps, rash, severe thirst, fainting, heat exhaustion and heat stroke.

rows.source: HSE workplace heat-stress and thermal-comfort control
rows.verified: Employers should remove or reduce heat sources where possible and use engineering controls such as ventilation, cooling or barriers.

rows.source: HSE workplace heat-stress and thermal-comfort control
rows.verified: Exposure duration and work rate can be reduced through mechanical aids, cooler work periods and planned rest breaks.

rows.source: HSE workplace heat-stress and thermal-comfort control
rows.verified: Cool drinking water should be provided and workers encouraged to drink frequently in small amounts.

rows.source: HSE workplace heat-stress and thermal-comfort control
rows.verified: Air temperature alone is not an adequate measure of thermal comfort because environmental, work and personal factors interact.

rows.source: HSE workplace heat-stress and thermal-comfort control
rows.verified: Workers should be consulted and workplace-temperature risks reassessed when discomfort or heat-stress symptoms are reported.

rows.source: HSE workplace heat-stress and thermal-comfort control
rows.verified: Heat risk depends on process heat, weather, humidity, work rate, clothing, PPE, acclimatisation, health and exposure duration.

rows.source: HSE workplace heat-stress and thermal-comfort control
rows.verified: HSE temperature evidence is workplace-, process-, worker-, clothing-, control- and time-specific and is not an exact parcel-level illness probability.
